tip: To give your name, Russian says зовут (zavut = they call) plus you in the object form: меня (menya = me). It reads 'me they-call'.
днём (dnyom = in the daytime) is the instrumental form used for time of day; the -ём (-yom) ending means 'during', no preposition needed.
To ask the time, Russian says который час (katoryy chas = which hour), literally 'which hour', not 'what time'.
свою (svayu = one's own) points back to the subject, so it fits any person. Use it, not мою (mayu = my), when the owner is the subject.
To say you speak a language, use the по- adverb: по-русски (pa-russki = in Russian). Lowercase and hyphenated, not the noun form.
Past-tense verbs agree with the speaker's gender: a woman says читала (chitala = read), a man says читал (chital).
нет (net = there isn't) forces the next noun into the genitive: телефона (telefona = of a phone). It marks the missing thing.
The tool you use goes in the instrumental with no preposition: левой рукой (levay rukoy = with the left hand). The -ой (-oy) ending means 'by means of'.
The -ся (-sya) on закрывается (zakryvaetsya = closes) makes it happen by itself; the museum does not close something, it just closes.
The person you write to goes in the dative: другу (drugu = to a friend). No separate word for 'to'; the -у (-u) ending carries it.
For an animate male object, accusative copies the genitive: хорошего стоматолога (kharosheva stamatolaga = a good dentist). The -его/-а (-eva/-a) endings mark it.
заниматься (zanimat'sya = to be occupied with) takes the instrumental, so 'what' becomes чем (chem): чем я занимаюсь (chem ya zanimayus' = what I do).
Age puts the person in the dative and drops the verb 'to be': бабушке (babushke = to grandmother) is eighty-five, literally 'to grandmother 85'.
Motion toward uses на (na) plus accusative: пришла на работу (prishla na rabotu = came to work); staying there is на работе (na rabote).
Feeling hot or cold uses the dative and no verb 'to be': мне (mne = to me) жарко (zharka = hot) means 'I am hot'.
около (okala = about) gives an approximate time or amount and takes the genitive: около двух часов (okala dvukh chasov = about two hours).
Minutes 'to' the hour use без (bez = without) plus the genitive: без десяти два (bez desyati dva = ten to two), literally 'without ten, two'.
Quantity words take the genitive: столько хлеба (stolka khleba = so much bread), not the plain form хлеб (khleb).
который (katoryy = who) takes its gender from человека (chelaveka = person) but its case from its own clause, here subject, so nominative.
To say how long an action took to finish, use за (za = in) plus the accusative: за час (za chas = in an hour).
For an action still going on, Russian keeps the present where English uses 'have been': жду уже (zhdu uzhe = I've already been waiting).
зачем (zachem = what for) asks about purpose, while почему (pachemu = why) asks about cause. Here it means 'what do you need it for'.
A date you do something 'on' takes the genitive: второго февраля (vtarova fevralya = on the second of February). No word for 'on' needed.
пока (paka = while) pairs with imperfective verbs for two things at once: ждал (zhdal = was waiting), читал (chital = was reading).
едет (edet = is riding) is one trip happening right now; ездит (ezdit = rides) would mean regular, repeated trips.
которую (katoruyu = which) is feminine to match книга (kniga = book), but accusative because it is the object of прочитал (prachital = read).
After 2, 3, 4 the noun is genitive singular, not plural: четыре книги (chetyre knigi = four books).
ли turns a statement into a yes/no question and attaches to the word being asked about: правда ли (pravda li = is it true).
Working 'as' a profession uses the instrumental: работает врачом (rabotaet vrachom = works as a doctor). The -ом (-om) ending replaces 'as a'.
For 'on' recurring days, use по (pa) plus the dative: по выходным (pa vykhadnym = on weekends). It marks a repeated schedule.
